notes.meaning: Paul reminds his readers that a law has authority over a person only while that person is alive. Once someone dies, that law no longer has any claim or control over them. He addresses his readers as people who understand this basic rule of law from daily life.

Paul uses marriage to illustrate how death ends legal obligations. A woman is bound by law to her husband as long as he lives, so being with another man during his lifetime makes her an adulteress. But if her husband dies, that marriage law is broken, and she is completely free to remarry without any guilt.

Believers have died to the law through the sacrificed body of Jesus on the cross. Because that old bond has ended, believers are now free to belong to the risen Christ. This new union enables Christians to live fruitful lives that truly please God.

Before coming to Christ, people lived under the control of their fallen human nature. God's good commandments actually stirred up rebellious passions in them, leading to sinful actions. The only final fruit of those actions was spiritual death.

Believers are now released from the law because they have died to what once held them captive. Instead of trying to obey external rules in their own strength, they now serve God in a fresh way through the Holy Spirit. This brings willing obedience from a changed heart rather than mere outward conformity.

Paul asks whether God's law is itself sinful, and he strongly rejects the thought. The law acts like a mirror that shows people the sin already inside them. For example, Paul says he would not have recognized that coveting—wrongly craving what belongs to others—was sin unless the law had explicitly forbidden it.

Sin took advantage of the commandment and used it as a starting place to stir up all kinds of wrong desires. Rebellious human nature naturally wants to do whatever is forbidden. Without the law exposing and provoking it, sin lay dormant and inactive.

Paul recalls a time when he felt spiritually secure and alive before the true demands of the law reached his heart. But when the commandment struck home, sin sprang to life with full power. At that moment, his self-righteous confidence collapsed, and he realized he was spiritually dead.

The commandment was originally given to point the way to life and blessing for anyone who obeyed it. But because fallen human beings cannot keep it, the law ended up pronouncing a sentence of death instead. The failure was not in God's holy rule, but in human weakness and disobedience.

Sin deceived Paul by misusing the commandment, just as the serpent tricked Eve in the garden of Eden. It promised happiness and freedom through disobedience, but it delivered only guilt and condemnation. In this way, sin used God's own commandment to bring about spiritual death.

Paul concludes that the law itself is completely holy, just, and good. Every commandment comes from God's pure nature and is designed for the good of humanity. The fault for human ruin belongs entirely to sin, never to God's law.

Paul rejects the idea that a good law could be the true cause of death. It was sin that produced death by twisting something good to its own evil ends. God permitted this so that sin would be exposed for what it really is: utterly destructive and evil.

The law is spiritual because it comes from God and requires pure motives, but human beings are fallen and weak. Paul describes feeling like a captive sold into slavery to sin, unable in himself to meet God's standard. This begins an intense description of the inner struggle between God's will and human weakness.

differ.view: Reformed Christians believe Paul is describing a normal, regenerate believer who recognizes the law's holiness and grieves over the sin that still clings to him.
Methodists teach that Paul is describing an unregenerate person under the law, struggling unsuccessfully against sin before finding full deliverance in Christ.
Lutherans see this verse as expressing the Christian life, in which the believer remains at the same time fully righteous by faith and a sinner in the flesh.

notes.meaning: Paul describes a confusing and painful split between his desires and his actions. He finds that he does not practice the good things he truly wishes to do. Instead, he ends up doing the very wrong things that he hates.

By hating the evil he commits, Paul shows that his conscience agrees with God's law. His desire to do the opposite proves that he recognizes the law as good and right. The blame rests entirely on his own failure, not on God's commandments.

Paul explains that when he sins against his better desires, it is driven by the principle of sin dwelling inside him. He is not excusing his wrongdoing or evading personal responsibility. Instead, he identifies sin as an unwelcome tyrant living within his fallen nature.

Paul acknowledges that nothing good lives in his natural, fallen flesh. He has the heartfelt desire to do what is right, but he lacks the strength in himself to carry it out. Good intentions alone are powerless to defeat indwelling sin.

Paul repeats his struggle to show how deep and persistent the problem really is. He fails to carry out the good he wants to do, and keeps falling into the evil he wants to avoid. This constant failure shows that knowing what is right does not give someone the power to perform it.

Because Paul acts against his own settled wish to do good, he traces the evil back to sin living inside him. His true desire opposes the deed, showing that sin has taken hold of his weaker nature. This proves once more that human willpower cannot conquer sin on its own.

Paul discovers a constant principle operating in his daily life. Whenever he resolves to do what is good, evil is right there beside him to pull him down. This tug-of-war is a regular pattern of human experience under the law.

In his inward self, Paul genuinely delights in God's holy law. His deepest thoughts, judgment, and affections agree with what God commands. This sincere love for God's ways points to a heart touched by divine truth.

differ.view: Methodists teach that even an unconverted person whose conscience is stirred by the law can admire God's commands without yet being born again.

notes.meaning: Paul sees another powerful force at work in his physical actions, fighting against the good desires of his mind. This sinful urge wages war within him and pulls him into captivity to sin. It creates a painful battle between what he knows is right and what his lower desires crave.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching identifies this warring impulse as concupiscence, the lingering pull toward sin that remains after baptism, which must be resisted but is not itself sin without consent.

notes.meaning: Weary of the constant struggle, Paul cries out in distress over his helpless condition. He asks who will rescue him from this body that is so weighed down by sin and death. It is the cry of a person who knows he cannot save himself and desperately needs a deliverer.

Paul bursts into praise because complete deliverance comes only through Jesus Christ our Lord. He then sums up the reality: with his mind he is devoted to serving God's law, but his fallen flesh still leans toward sin. True victory is found not in human effort, but through Christ alone.

differ.view: Reformed Christians see this summary as proof that even mature believers live in this tension until death, serving God with the mind while fighting the flesh.
Methodists believe this summary looks back on the struggle under the law, whereas the true Christian is freed from this divided slavery through the Spirit in Romans 8.
